items.question: Why do you see AI creativity as the real promise of AI?
items.object: AI creativity and the promise of AI beyond automation
items.answer: A lot of times, when we talk about AI, both in the Valley and elsewhere, I think there's a conflation between AI and automation. AI can absolutely automate things; there's no doubt about that, especially routine things. But I think that honestly undersells the real promise of AI. I think the real promise of AI is what Demis Hassabis of DeepMind calls AI creativity: it's the ability to acquire knowledge that did not exist before. I experienced this firsthand. The reason why I'm such a true believer in the technology is because, again, I was the expert who helped design the system, but this very AI agent that we created is telling me new things about the system that I didn't know about before. That's a very, very powerful feeling.

items.question: How did Andrew Ng’s Introduction to Machine Learning course on Coursera shape your interest in machine learning?
items.object: Andrew Ng’s Introduction to Machine Learning course on Coursera
items.answer: I had been experimenting as part of my famed 20% time at Google with machine learning technologies. A very specific course, Introduction to Machine Learning by Andrew Ng on Coursera, had just come out. This was back in 2013. I think I was, like, the second cohort or something, and that class had completely changed my life. I taught myself how to program and just started tinkering around with machine learning on the side. It was very interesting technology.

items.question: How did AlphaGo shape your thinking about applying reinforcement learning to Google's data centers?
items.object: Applying reinforcement learning to Google's data centers
items.answer: My responsibility at the time was to, one, help Google design and operate their very large data centers. Once these very large data centers, which consume enormous amounts of energy, were built, we shifted our focus to operating these complex industrial systems in the most energy-efficient way possible because they use billions of dollars in electricity. That was the background. I was already tinkering around with machine learning technologies on the side to analyze the enormous amounts of data Google's data centers were generating. In 2016, AlphaGo came out, and I was one of hundreds of millions of people around the world watching it. It was, like, 1:00 a.m. in the Bay Area or something, and I found it absolutely captivating. I sent an email to Moose describing this idea: if DeepMind could beat the smartest, most intelligent people in the world at complex games like Go, then surely we can train these same AI agents to play a very different game that I'm familiar with called, “Let's optimize the PUE, the power usage effectiveness, of Google's data centers.” That was the context for that email. I remember internally the way I pitched it to Google's leadership, specifically Joe Kava, who leads Google's data centers and operations: I showed a picture of a Go board on one side and a video game controller, like an Xbox controller, on the other. I'm like, look, there are objective functions that we're trying to minimize or maximize; there are concrete knobs and levers, so actions that we can control; there are constraints that we have to stay within; and all of this happens within a very measurable environment. I think reinforcement learning and operating large, complex industrial systems are actually one and the same thing. That was the original kernel of insight that inspired it all.

items.question: How do you determine whether a real-world control problem can be solved using reinforcement learning?
items.object: Applying reinforcement learning to real-world control problems
items.answer: Reinforcement learning systems need KPIs to optimize for. They need to know how good or bad an action is. They obviously need things to control, and they need to know what constraints they have to stay within. As long as we can map the problem we're trying to solve into a reinforcement learning framework—which, from a mathematical perspective, means we're solving a constrained optimization problem—if you can define the constrained optimization problem and map it to the underlying data, it should be able to be solved using reinforcement learning. That's very much the lens through which we look at things at Phaidra as well.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between reinforcement learning and the fields of controls and optimization?
items.object: The relationship between reinforcement learning and controls and optimization
items.answer: We often talk about how reinforcement learning and controls and optimization are two wildly different fields historically that have somehow independently converged to the same area. They're two very similar concepts, but we've been calling them by different names this whole time. You've had these independent evolutions, different ways of tackling the same problem, and Phaidra is really the intersection of both of these.

items.question: How confident were you that reinforcement learning could work for operating a data center?
items.object: Applying reinforcement learning to industrial operations
items.answer: I didn't even know if it was going to work. Conceptually, it made sense in my mind. Operating a data center is just a different game to play, and there's all kinds of different games in the industrial world. Maybe the game is maximize energy efficiency; maybe the game is minimize water consumption; maybe the game is maximize the yield of a factory. There's all these games that we're constantly playing. In my mind it made sense, but, to answer your question directly, no, I had no idea if it was going to work.

items.question: What convinced you that the AI optimizing your data center was creative?
items.object: AI creativity demonstrated through data center optimization
items.answer: I still vividly remember to this day when we turned on the AI system and watched the energy just drop. It was so surprising for two reasons. Number one, we had designed the system. I played a role in designing that very mechanical system that the AI was now controlling and optimizing. In theory, I'm literally supposed to be the subject matter expert who knows everything about these systems, but the AI is teaching me things that I didn't know about the system I helped design in the first place. Two, the moves that the AI was making were very counterintuitive. When we looked at the decisions coming out, we looked at the plant operators and thought to ourselves, “There's no way this is right. This AI sucks. I learned the wrong thing, but we're here anyway, so let's try what the AI is saying.” We tried it, and it worked, and we saw the energy plummet. That was when I became a believer in this technology: fundamentally, this technology is creative. It helps us discover new knowledge that didn't exist before from raw data.

items.question: What surprised you about the energy-efficiency gains from using AI to control a data center?
items.object: Software-driven energy-efficiency gains from AI control of a data center
items.answer: It respected exactly the same constraints as the plant operators and engineers had already put in place. This is pure gain, respecting exactly the same temperature profiles, the same constraints around how quickly you can turn on and off a chiller, minimum pump VFD speeds, all that sort of stuff. This is pure optimization, pure gain, which I think is one of those crazy things. We don't really expect it. Usually, when you think about energy efficiency, people think about expensive capex: “Oh, we've got to rip out the chillers, buy a bunch of new chillers from Johnson Controls and Trane or whatever, and install them.” Those are hardware efficiency gains. You don't really think about pure software, data-driven efficiency gains. I think that's part of what was surprising for us.

items.question: Why do you think complex industrial facilities have so much undiscovered potential for efficiency improvements through technologies like AlphaGo?
items.object: Undiscovered efficiency improvements in industrial control systems
items.answer: I often tell folks to do a simple thought experiment. Imagine you have just 10 machines you're controlling, say pumps, and each one has 10 possible set point values, or 10 modes associated with it, like 10% pump speed, 20% pump speed, 30% pump speed, et cetera. In this very simple toy example, you have 10 to the 10, or 10 billion, different permutations for how you can operate your toy system. Then the question becomes: at any given point, what is the most optimal way of operating your toy system? These are dynamic systems. The IT load is changing, the weather is fluctuating, the people operating these systems are changing, the pipes are corroding, and the heat exchangers are fouling. These are very complex dynamic systems. Real-world systems have a lot more than 10 machines, and each machine has a lot more than 10 set points. You can start seeing why technologies like AlphaGo, which manage to navigate immense complexity, are helpful here. It also helps explain why there's often so much room for optimization in the first place, because there's so much complexity. If you think about the total action space—all the possible actions within a modern data center, for example—because of risk averseness, but also because of hardcoded rules and heuristics, we've only ever explored 0.00001% of all the possible ways you could operate that system. What is in this 99.99999% of the action space we've never explored? Surely there are more optimal ways of operating the system than what we've done historically. That's an intuitive explanation of why there can be such large efficiency improvements in the first place that are undiscovered.

items.question: Why do you see limitations in how industrial facilities are operated today?
items.object: Human intuition and hardcoded control logic in industrial facilities
items.answer: The way we operate these facilities is constrained by a mixture of hardcoded control logic. Don't get me wrong, these are automated systems today already; they're just not operated intelligently, I would argue. There is a healthy mixture of human intuition as well, where we have people like myself or plant operators constantly monitoring the system, nudging the system, adjusting things, or setting the rules—the constraints that the system has to operate within. Fundamentally, human intuition plus hardcoded control logic is still limited when you talk about this degree of complexity.

items.question: How did you come to see direct AI control as the next step after Google’s 2016 data center pilot?
items.object: Google’s transition from an AI recommendation pilot to autonomous data center control
items.answer: There are two types of results. For Google in particular, there were the results from the pilot. In 2016, we announced the pilot. The pilot was done on a couple of data centers, but fundamentally it was not an autonomous control system. What I mean by this is the AI was generating recommendations for human experts like myself to manually review and implement. Of course, we didn't want to jump straight to taking our hands off the steering wheel because it was a new, novel technology. Also, no one knew at the time: is it even possible to use AI from the cloud to control big-ass infrastructure? Step one was do the pilot. They had generated recommendations. That's where we saw really steep, like, 40% energy savings. That experience taught us, “Hey, we think there's something real over here. We should actually just let the AI control things directly to get the value automatically.” Quite frankly, the plant operators were getting tired of checking their email every 15 minutes, waiting for the AI to tell them what to do. They had better things to do. So we decided—or rather, operations and Joe decided—“Hey, it's time to go to a fully automated system.” This was total uncharted territory. We didn't even know if it was possible to control machines from the cloud, huge industrial infrastructure in the cloud, because to our knowledge no one had done it before.

items.object: The first demonstration of controlling a chiller from the cloud
items.answer: The chiller that we were standing right next to roars to life. As it's coming to life, the ground is shaking vigorously. Now the next question is, how do we control things intelligently from the cloud, where all the compute resources are?

items.question: Where do you think AI’s ability to discover new knowledge will have the greatest impact?
items.object: AI creativity and the discovery of new knowledge
items.answer: A lot of times, when we talk about AI, both in the Valley and elsewhere, I think there's a conflation between AI and automation. AI can absolutely automate things; there's no doubt about that, especially routine things. But I think that honestly undersells the real promise of AI. I think the real promise of AI is what Demis Hassabis of DeepMind calls AI creativity: it's the ability to acquire knowledge that did not exist before. I experienced this firsthand. The reason why I'm such a true believer in the technology is because, again, I was the expert who helped design the system, but this very AI agent that we created is telling me new things about the system that I didn't know about before. That's a very, very powerful feeling. It's kind of like when you think back to AlphaGo. Lee Sedol was the best in his field at Go. He was the world champion for a decade. He was at the top, and his ELO rating was just something outrageous, like 2,800 or something. It was outrageously high, but it had flatlined for a full decade. His ELO rating was the same, and there was no one to challenge him because he was already at the top. Once he hit the top, he just plateaued. After AlphaGo happened, and he got to play against AlphaGo privately a few more times because DeepMind had let him continue interacting with the system, for the first time in a decade his ELO rating started climbing. This is what I mean when I say the real power of AI is helping us discover knowledge that we didn't necessarily know about before. Where you're going to see the most gain from that is not going to be in routine automation things like call centers. It's going to be in very complex areas, where human intuition is insufficient because of immense complexity, but that are underpinned by data. That's why you're seeing things like protein folding. That's extraordinary. It's those areas of massive permutational complexity underpinned by data where I think we're going to see some of the most interesting companies and products.

items.question: Why do you see turning AI technology into a product as essential to achieving real impact?
items.object: Turning AI technology into a product
items.answer: The other lesson my co-founders and I learned is around this: if you want real impact, you have to turn the technology into a product. This is the core reason why we decided to leave DeepMind and train technologies to start Phaidra. Over and over again, we were seeing the technologies we were helping to develop at DeepMind were extraordinary, achieving crazy things like protein folding. The problem is, in order for the technology to make the most impact, you have to get it into the real world; people have to actually use it. That fundamentally means we're talking about a product. Turning a technology into a product is a hundredfold, a thousandfold more work, and that led us to the conclusion that it's time to leave and start a company that creates these intelligent virtual plant operators, these intelligent AI agents, as a real product.

items.question: How do you understand the challenge of applying your Google DeepMind experience across different industrial customers?
items.object: Learning from the diversity of industrial customers and facilities
items.answer: The problem, though, is that the real world is quite diverse. Every single customer is diverse, and especially when you talk about industrial facilities, every industrial facility is a snowflake. The learnings have been massive since we left Google and DeepMind, because every time we onboard a new customer we're learning something new about how equipment are connected, or some product gap we didn't know about that needs to be fixed, or new ways that data can break. I can tell you a hundred different ways that data with mission-critical cooling systems can break. Probably not the most interesting party topic for most folks, but I personally find it quite interesting. There's certainly been quite a lot of learning in that regard.

items.question: Why do you think the industrial AI work you pioneered at Google and DeepMind could only have been done at a company like Google?
items.object: Google's suitability for pioneering real-time industrial AI
items.answer: When I look back, I think what we helped pioneer at Google and DeepMind could only have been done at a company like Google. Google is a very forward-leaning company, but one of the things I've learned is Google is absolutely an anomaly when it comes to how much data it has, the pristine quality of the data, and the ease of access to the data. Google is fundamentally a data analytics company and invested in all this infrastructure in high-quality, high-availability data on which you can do real-time intelligence applications like what we were doing. There are many other examples of this within Google and DeepMind. Having left the nest, one of our rude awakenings was that Google is definitely an anomaly.

items.question: How do you assess industrial customers' readiness to let AI autonomously control their facilities?
items.object: Industrial customers' readiness for autonomous AI control
items.answer: Everyone is in various states of their AI journey. Google is on one extreme. We've encountered customers where, forget about real-time intelligence, they're not capturing the data in the first place. They may be sensorized—in the industries we work with, like pharmaceuticals and district cooling, and especially data centers, almost always the customer is sensorized because these are billion-dollar facilities and it makes sense to throw a million dollars' worth of sensors on them. But just because you sensor it doesn't mean you're storing the data. A lot of our customers aren't storing the data beyond 90 days or six months or a year. They might cite reasons like, “Well, it's costly to store the data,” or, more commonly, “We're not using the data for anything,” which is true. A lot of our industrial customers aren't using the data. It's more a forensics thing: if something goes wrong, we go back and look at the logs to see what happened. If we think about Maslow's hierarchy of data needs, you've got your sensorization, then storage, then you have to invest in making sure the data is cleaned. There's a lot of effort around making sure the data is actually cleaned and usable. That requires you to know what bad data looks like, what good data looks like, and how to convert bad data into good data so it's useful. Once you have clean data, you also need to make it accessible in a streaming and batch historical manner. There are different gradients of AI readiness. The customers we work with are all over the spectrum, but Phaidra today is at the point where we are autonomously controlling data centers for our customers.

items.question: What do you think defines the fourth Industrial Revolution?
items.object: The fourth Industrial Revolution
items.answer: The '70s and '80s was the third Industrial Revolution. With that was the shift from analog to digital and the advent of the first automation systems. In order to automate, you fundamentally first have to sensorize. These are simple automation systems. The fourth Industrial Revolution—we're biased, but at Phaidra we think the fourth Industrial Revolution means intelligent infrastructure: infrastructure that can operate itself and fundamentally get better over time at doing so, self-improving infrastructure.

items.question: How do you think AI should fit into existing industrial control systems?
items.object: Integrating AI into existing industrial control systems
items.answer: Right now we're shoehorning intelligence into systems from the third Industrial Revolution, so they certainly weren't designed for this. What we do instead is, most importantly, ride on top of the existing control system. There is a hardcoded layer of rules and heuristics, millions of lines of if-then statements programmed into what we would typically call the BMS, the building management system, or a SCADA system, that defines how the facility should operate. The problem with hardcoded systems is that because they're hardcoded, they operate the same way today as they did yesterday, a year ago, or five years ago—more like 10 years ago, because people don't very frequently go into the backend programming to update that control logic. What Phaidra does is insert a new cloud intelligence layer at the very top of the control stack. We don't introduce any hardware or new sensorization; we ride on top of the existing control stack. That's really critical. You can think of it as a general in the battlefield. The general has a global view of everything happening across the system and is issuing command signals to the troops on the ground for actual execution. The AI is looking at 10,000 trends a minute in real time and issuing decisions like which pumps to turn on or what their pump speed should be to the local BMS system and/or the PLCs for automatic implementation and execution. Were they designed for this in the first place? No. There's a lot of work we have to do with our customers to be able to accept this type of external intelligence. There's a lot of work we do in defining the safety nets and guardrails to ensure that the AI can't do bad things to the customer system. Fundamentally, we are still riding on top of the existing controls architecture, and we always want to do that. You don't want AI controlling things like how fast a valve opens and shuts. That's a terrible application of AI; hardcoded rules and heuristics will do great there. If you look at the overall system, 90% of it is fine with hardcoded rules and heuristics because it's granular control logic that doesn't need non-deterministic, crazy-powerful intelligence behind it.

items.question: How do you think customers should judge the value of reinforcement learning for industrial control beyond its initial energy savings?
items.object: Reinforcement learning’s long-term value in industrial control
items.answer: What I always tell our customers is don't over-index on the magnitude of the energy savings initially. We honestly have no idea ahead of time what the energy savings or reliability improvements are going to be, because these are non-deterministic systems. By definition, if I could tell you what things you're not doing in order to get energy savings, why do you need the AI in the first place? What we do know is that the unique thing about this technology, about reinforcement learning in particular, is that it is a closed-loop system, a self-learning system. It can learn because it's able to take actions and measure the impact of its actions against its predictions, and that means it gets better over time. Maybe we start off at 1% energy savings, maybe 5%, maybe 10%, but fundamentally it will learn and get better over time. Not infinitely, because there are laws of physics, but it will get better over time, and once it reaches optimal, it will stay at optimal. That's super important, because with hardcoded rules and heuristics, when you tuned a system as you were commissioning it, when you're turning it on for the first time, that system today no longer performs the same way it did 10 years ago when you first commissioned it, because the pipes have corroded, the heat exchangers have fouled, the cooling towers have scaled, or you ripped out equipment. The promise of an adaptive, self-learning system is that it will change with you. As your customers are putting in a bunch of H100 and soon H200 GPUs, the system will learn and adapt on the fly with you, so it can stay optimal.

items.question: How do you understand the concentration of real-world reinforcement learning applications in big tech companies?
items.object: Real-world reinforcement learning applications and their concentration in big tech
items.answer: Unfortunately, my knowledge is very heavily indexed on the Google and DeepMind space because that's what we spent so much time on. Even within Google and DeepMind, there were other very cool reinforcement learning applications. For example, the team that sat right next to us used RL systems to help prolong battery life. You may notice that your Android phone's battery life has been increasing. There are hardware changes associated with that, but there are also intelligent software changes behind the scenes that proactively manage your battery life. There were reinforcement learning systems for YouTube video recommendations, and a whole host of other things. Absolutely, there are reinforcement learning applications in the wild. To your point, though, I wouldn't say there are a whole lot of them. I think it's not a coincidence that you tend to see them at more of the big tech companies, where they've already invested in the data infrastructure so they can benefit from this technology. Outside of the big tech companies, there are very few applications of real-world reinforcement learning in production, at least.

items.question: How do you assess the potential scope of reinforcement learning applications?

items.answer: I think the applications for reinforcement learning are freaking massive, and Phaidra is one of many examples. items.question: How do you see the potential of AI to coordinate data-center electricity loads and help balance the grid?
items.object: Coordinating data-center electricity loads to balance the grid
items.answer: Oh my gosh, that would be wild. I think it's not so much about the magnitude of the energy savings per se, but rather the potential cost savings, because then you could start shifting your loads around to when it's most cost-effective to do compute. Or if you had CO2 signals, you could start scheduling loads around when it's the least carbon-intensive to do your non-latency-sensitive workloads, which I think Google has already been experimenting with a bit. Honestly, I think it's really more around global system-level optimization. We have to keep in mind that data centers already are, but increasingly are, massive load banks. Data centers were 1.5% or 2% of U.S. energy consumption; that's about to increase to 4% this year, I think, and by the end of the decade is projected to get up to 9% of U.S. energy. In Ireland, right now, 22% of Ireland's national electricity consumption goes to data centers alone. The International Energy Agency predicts that's going to increase to 37% by the end of the decade. Mind-boggling numbers. The reason why I mention this is because these are massive load banks on the grid. There is an actual opportunity, if you could somehow coordinate the data centers together, to help balance the grid. That is such a gnarly challenge, and it is what is holding the energy transition back. As more and more renewable energy starts coming onto the grid, the supply side becomes increasingly stochastic. We used to have this perfectly deterministic system, at least on the supply side, where a good operator could call someone who operates a coal-fired power plant and say, “Hey, ramp up or down your power production.” Deterministic.

items.question: How do you understand the effect of increasing renewable energy penetration on the grid's need for reserve capacity?
items.object: Renewable energy penetration and reserve capacity on the electricity grid
items.answer: As you get more and more renewable penetration coming onto the grid, you have a somewhat non-deterministic demand side—it's somewhat predictable, but there are definitely spikes—and a massively non-deterministic supply side. The problem is that because we do not know how much energy we're going to generate, you now have all this wasted excess capacity in reserve. There's a concept of spinning reserves on the grid, where there are peaker plants, giant natural gas turbines, that as we speak are just sitting there idling, like your car idles at a stoplight, in case we need that power as a buffer against uncertainty. As renewable penetration increases, ironically, the amount of buffer you need also increases. If you look at Germany's failed energy transition, they decommissioned their nuclear baseload while ramping up their renewable energy penetration.

items.question: How do you see transformers and reinforcement learning complementing each other in industrial control applications like Phaidra's?
items.object: The complementary strengths of transformers and reinforcement learning for industrial control
items.answer: My co-founder Vaha is by far the expert on this topic. He knows way, way more than me. I'm just a simple mechanical engineer who happened to learn a bit about AI. I think the intersection is really interesting: very potentially complementary strengths and weaknesses is how I would describe it. It's certainly not mutually exclusive. I was just talking with V about this earlier. V will tell you that all intelligence systems have certain hallmarks of intelligence so that we can say they are intelligent. They need to deeply understand the world, the environment that they're modeling. There needs to be some element of memory, remembering things, and, very importantly, there needs to be the ability to plan and reason. Transformers are clearly quite good at the first one, in the sense that they can take in huge amounts of structured and unstructured data to learn quite good models of the world. But it's limited in the sense that these models are primarily through correlation and not causation. That makes it challenging, at least for what Phaidra does, because we work with real-world systems. We have to have causality. We have to understand why the AI is doing certain things, why it's not doing other things, and how do we force a certain behavior that we know has to exist in our system. These are mission-critical systems; there has to be causality. That's where the limitation is. With reinforcement learning systems, the power of RL-based systems is much in the planning and reasoning part, where you're able to plan long trajectories of actions and learn intricate policies. I think where it gets really interesting is the intersection, where potentially transformer architectures can learn models, like value functions.

items.question: What most excites you about the development of AI applications over the next five to ten years?
items.object: AI applications over the next five to ten years
items.answer: In the very near future, I'm excited about the absolute explosion of AI applications. It feels kind of like a Precambrian explosion of sorts, where there's a primordial soup and all these AI startups and services are all of a sudden springing up. It's quite exciting. But when I look at where that activity is happening, where that research and entrepreneurial activity is happening, it's very clearly focused around LLMs and, even more specifically, natural language interactions, text-based interactions. That certainly is a large part of the economy and is very exciting, but in the five-to-10-year frame, I'm most excited about when we can start getting some of this technology into real-world physical applications. It's the intersection of this technology with the real-world infrastructure that we live in: big industrial systems, cars, homes, physical things.

items.question: Why do you admire your former DeepMind boss Moose’s ability to turn technology into products?
items.object: Moose’s ability to turn technology into products
items.answer: I admire Moose a lot, my old boss, who has of course since moved over to Microsoft. One of the biggest lessons my co-founders and I learned at DeepMind is that making a technology like what we did for Google data centers versus making a product like what we're doing at Phaidra are totally different things, wildly, wildly different things. There are few people as good in the world as Moose at taking technologies and turning them into real products. I remember my co-founder Katie and I were sitting down, grabbing drinks with Moose at some random dive bar in Seattle. He happened to be up there, before OpenAI released ChatGPT-2 and ushered in a world of craziness. He was raving to us about the applications of LLMs and how powerful these systems are, and we were like, “Okay, Moose, but let us tell you about Phaidra.” We had no idea what he was talking about. He was prescient; he saw this ages in advance, the technology that was being developed and the capabilities it would usher in. Then, of course, he went off and started Inflection. I admire him a lot for the ability to turn technology into actual products.

items.question: Why do you think having co-founders is so important when starting a company?
items.object: Having co-founders when starting a company
items.answer: My advice there is: make sure you have co-founders. This is so stressful; so many things can go wrong, and you're constantly on this emotional roller coaster of ups and downs. Having co-founders to lean on, both for the workload and for emotional support and mental sanity, is so important.
quotes: My advice there is twofold. One, make sure you have co-founders. This is so stressful; so many things can go wrong, and you're constantly on this emotional roller coaster of ups and downs. Having co-founders to lean on, both for the workload and for emotional support and mental sanity, is so important.

rubrics.text: The response explains that co-founders help founders cope with the emotional strain of starting a company.

items.question: How do you assess the risk of leaving a well-paid job with a promising career trajectory to start a company?
items.object: The risk of leaving a successful career to start a company
items.answer: The risk is less than you think it is. I'm biased, but I think people should take the jump. A lot of times when I talk with my former colleagues and other people thinking about making the jump, they'll say things like, “I've got a nice job over here; they pay me well; I'm on a rising trajectory.” My point is always that, no matter how valuable and successful you are today in the organization, you will only be more valuable and successful for that organization, other organizations, or society in general if you learn new skill sets. Take the plunge. Go out, start a company, learn what it's like to turn technologies into products. If that fails for whatever reason, hopefully it doesn't, the Googles and Microsofts of the world will only want to hire you back at an even higher premium. So why not take the plunge?

rubrics.text: The response states that skills gained from starting a company can increase a founder’s value to employers even if the company fails.
